claims.text: Applying a thin aluminide coating to a boride-based component will improve its resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
The aluminide coating forms a stable, aluminum-rich barrier.
The aluminum-rich barrier limits interdiffusion and chemical attack.
Uncoated boride-based component surfaces are prone to corrosive attack in molten aluminum.
Pack cementation or an equivalent vapor-deposition method can generate an approximately micron-scale aluminum-rich diffusion barrier on the component surface.
Typical hot-dip aluminum-plating exposure occurs at approximately 700–750°C in an aluminum melt.
The intervention will produce a dense, uniform aluminide layer.
The aluminide layer reduces aluminum diffusion.
The aluminide layer limits the reactive interface between molten aluminum and the boride substrate.
An aluminum-rich surface minimizes the chemical gradients that drive aggressive interdiffusion between molten aluminum and the underlying boride.
The aluminide barrier reduces the kinetics of corrosive interfacial reactions.
Reducing corrosive interfacial reaction kinetics lowers the overall corrosion rate.
Aluminide-coated components will exhibit a lower corrosion rate than uncoated components under identical molten-aluminum exposure.
Aluminide-coated components will exhibit shallower corrosion penetration than uncoated components under identical molten-aluminum exposure.
The predicted improvement will remain effective at 700–750°C for typical exposure durations.
